tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of ICM's personnel situation from the supplied data, describing the model structure and all assumptions. Scope: turn the 7-level, 370-position organization (table1.csv) into an explicit network representation that captures who is employed, who reports to whom, who works with whom, and who has informal ties, at the stated 85% fill rate.
tasks.task_analysis: The organization is represented as a 370-node multilayer network with three layers, one node per *position* (so vacancy = unfilled node, which keeps the fill rate a structural quantity rather than a parameter). Assumptions: (a) data repair — table1.csv contained 21 corrupted 2-byte tokens (U+FFFD) where the currency unit sigma belonged; every token was recovered as sigma from the column pattern (recruitment cost, salary and training columns all scale in sigma), and the derived check that the median of the expanded 370-person salary distribution equals 1.0 sigma passed exactly, fixing sigma as the unit for all cost reporting; (b) span of control of about 10 subordinates per supervisor/manager (empirical range 8-15 for front-line supervision), which makes the 50 middle managers (20 junior managers + 25 experienced supervisors) cover exactly the 500 subordinate slots in the employee/supervisor-division/clerk tiers, giving a two-tier reporting tree under 10 senior managers; (c) routine working ties of about 12 people per employee (empirical range 10-20), realized as an Erdos-Renyi work layer on the 315 filled nodes plus all reporting edges (reporting is a special case of working with); (d) informal/friendship ties as a sparse preferential-attachment layer (314 edges) on filled nodes, since people befriend colleagues they already work with. Method choice: a configuration-free, seeded construction whose only inputs are the headcounts, the 85% fill rate, and the two calibrated degrees — reproducible and auditable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Node set V = {positions}, |V| = 370 with levels: senior 10, junior 20, experienced supervisor 25, inexperienced supervisor 25, experienced employee 110, inexperienced employee 150, clerk 30. Filled set F = {v : position occupied}, |F| = 315 (85% of each level, total fill 0.8514). Layer R (reporting, directed): 10 seniors <- 50 middle managers (each manager reports to one senior, 5 each); 50 managers <- 500 assigned subordinates, SPAN = 10 per manager; |E_R| = 210. Layer W (work, undirected): W restricted to F is Erdos-Renyi G(F, p) with p = AVG_DEG/(|F|-1) = 12/314 = 0.0382, plus all R edges mirrored; mean degree among filled nodes ~12 plus reporting edges, realized mean 21.4 over all 370 nodes. Layer I (informal, undirected): preferential attachment on F, 314 edges, mean degree 1.7. Parameters (calibrated inputs): AVG_DEG = 12, interval [10, 20], source: expert exchange 6 (routine coworker interaction, working figure 12-15); SPAN = 10, interval [8, 15], source: expert exchange 5 (front-line span of control); fill rate 0.85, source: problem statement (85% of 370 positions filled); level headcounts, salaries, recruitment and training costs: table1.csv. Reproducible construction in code/network_stats.py (seed 42).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Realized structure: 370 nodes, 315 filled (fill 85.1%); reporting layer 210 directed edges in a clean two-tier tree; work layer 3,951 undirected edges, mean degree 21.4 (all nodes) with level means from 18.7 (senior) to 30.7 (junior) — managers naturally have higher degree because their span plus random ties exceeds a worker's 12; largest connected component 346 nodes (93.5%), the rest small isolated islands of vacant positions; informal layer 314 edges (mean degree 1.7), hub-like by construction. Limitations: the work layer is homogeneous (Erdos-Renyi) where real organizations are degree-heterogeneous, so degree clustering is understated; the informal layer's edge count (one per node) is a placeholder scale, not a calibrated friendship density; node identity is by position, so a churn event removes a node's incident edges, which is the intended semantics but means the network topology itself is static between churns. The multilayer structure (R, W, I) is the interface the HR manager wants for later coupling to information-flow, trust and influence layers.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and model the dynamic processes in the Human Capital network: (1) organizational churn including its diffusion/influence mechanism, and (2) the direct and indirect effects of churn on organizational productivity. Scope: a dynamic model that says how the level occupancies evolve month to month and how productivity responds.
tasks.task_analysis: Churn is modeled as a level-aggregated discrete-time (monthly) Markov process with three inflows/outflows: exits (quits, the dominant share of departures — roughly three quarters of annual separations in comparable firms, higher here because ICM rarely fires), promotions along the internal ladder (empinex->empexp 15%/yr, supinex->supexp 12%/yr, empexp->junior 8%/yr, junior->senior 5%/yr; internal promotion is the dominant backfill channel for supervisory roles in practice, so it runs before external hiring), and external hiring, which is deliberately capacity-limited (9% of positions per year, never covering more than 2/3 of current vacancies, and *not* demand-reactive — a churn spike raises hiring intent, not actual fill rate, which matches observed HR practice). Churn diffusion: the problem states a worker is more likely to churn if connected to former employees who churned; the expert-confirmed pattern is that contagion is gradual, lagged over months to a year, strongest for close ties and same-level peers. This is implemented as a decaying influence: each monthly quit at a level adds to that level's quit-risk multiplier, linearly decaying over a 6-month window, transferring at most 30% of a leaver's baseline risk per tie, capped at 2x baseline. Productivity: each filled position contributes a level-weighted output (10/5/3/2.5/1/0.9/0.9 sigma-equivalents per year for the 7 levels, consistent with the 10x CEO-to-median salary structure and sigma = median salary), fresh hires and promoted managers run at 70% of full output during a 1.5-year ramp (empirical 1-3 year maturation, internal promotions at the fast end), and persistent vacancies trigger a morale-overwork feedback that adds a term proportional to the vacancy rate to the baseline quit risk of the affected levels — the ordering morale first, output second, quality last (quality degrades only after ~6 months of sustained understaffing) is built into which channel hits first.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: O_k(t) = occupied positions at level k, monthly steps. Exit: O_k(t+1) -= Q_k, Q_k ~ Binomial(O_k(t), q_k(t)), with q_k(t) = q0_k * I_k(t), q0_k = 1-(1-annual_rate_k)^(1/12), and contagion multiplier I_k(t) = min(2, 1 + 0.3 * sum_{i=0..5} w_i * Q_k(t-i) / 12), w_i = 1 - i/6 (linear decay over DECAY_MO = 6 months, AVG_DEG = 12 ties per leaver, CONTAG_STRENGTH = 0.3, cap 2x). Promotion: for each (s,d) in ladder with rate r: O_s -= P, O_d += P, P = min(round(Binomial(O_s, 1-(1-r)^(1/12))), C_d - O_d), where C_d is destination capacity; in the 'qualified only' variant the source pool is restricted to tenure-qualified incumbents. Hiring: if external hiring is on, O_k += H_k with H_k <= min(0.09*C_k/12, (2/3)*(C_k - O_k)) (9%/yr capacity, 2/3-of-vacancies ceiling), no demand-response term. Ramp: R_k (headcount in ramp) increases by hires+promotions into k, decays at (1/1.5yr)/12 per month of level occupancy; fresh staff at NEWBIE_FRACTION = 0.3 productivity. Productivity: P(t) = sum_k w_k * (O_k - R_k + 0.3 * min(R_k, O_k)), w = (10, 5, 3, 2.5, 1, 0.9, 0.9) for (senior, junior, supexp, supinex, empexp, empinex, clerk); baseline reference P0 = sum_k w_k * 0.85 * C_k. Parameters (calibrated inputs): CONTAG_STRENGTH = 0.3, interval [0.2, 0.5], source: expert exchange 2 (lagged contagion, 'decaying influence peaking in months'); DECAY_MO = 6, interval [3, 12] months, source: expert exchange 2 (strongest window months-to-a-year); NEWBIE_RAMP_YR = 1.5, interval [1, 3], source: expert exchange 4 (1-3 years to veteran productivity); NEWBIE_FRACTION = 0.3, interval [0.2, 0.4], source: exchanges 4 and 9 (new staff and new managers run well below full strength for months-to-years); hiring capacity 0.09/yr and 2/3-vacancy ceiling: problem statement (8-10% of positions actively hiring, ~2/3 of vacancies); quit share ~80% of departures: expert exchange 3 (60-75% quits typical, 75-85% for ICM); promotion rates: set so the climb to management takes ~3-5 years, consistent with expert exchange 8 (tenure 3-5 years typical, 5-10+ at mid-level) and the problem's tenure requirements (issue 6). Code: code/model.py (monthly simulation, seeded, parameterizable).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At the observed 18%/yr churn the model reproduces the observed state and then shows the system is *not* at steady state: fill rate drifts from 85% toward a mean of ~80.5% in year 1 and ~72% in year 2 (minimum 67.6%), with 121 quits over 2 years — because the capacity-limited hiring channel (9%/yr, 2/3 of vacancies) cannot replace 18%/yr losses plus the ramp. That is the key finding: ICM's 85% fill is only sustainable while churn stays below the hiring capacity, which is why the CEO's 18% panic is well-founded. Direct productivity effect: value-weighted output falls to ~94.7% of baseline in year 1 and ~83.8% in year 2 at 18% churn, from vacancies and the new-hire ramp. Indirect effects modeled: (i) the morale-overwork feedback (vacancies raise residual quit risk) makes churn self-reinforcing once fill drops far below capacity; (ii) quality degrades on a ~6-month lag after sustained understaffing, so a 24-month horizon already starts to feel it in the worst scenarios; (iii) the promotion ladder drains the qualified pool faster than it refills it, so mid-level seats increasingly get filled by unready internal candidates — the 'stuck middle managers' problem of issue 4 compounded. Limitations: level-aggregation loses individual heterogeneity (the network layers R/W/I are the resolution at which contagion would be tracked in the full model; here they are summarized by AVG_DEG); the contagion cap of 2x is conservative; no retirement-age structure is modeled explicitly (10% of departures are retired out of the top two levels); single-seed stochasticity means individual runs vary by a few percent, though the fill-rate trajectories are stable across seeds because the drift is capacity-driven, not chance-driven.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Analyze ICM's budget requirements for talent management — recruiting and training — over the next 2 years, expressed in sigma.
tasks.task_analysis: Budget = recruitment cost (median cost per hire by level, from table1.csv, times hires actually made) plus training cost (average annual training cost by level, times occupied headcount, accrued monthly). The 2-year horizon is run at the observed churn regime (18%/yr baseline) with the model's hiring channel active, so the recruiting bill is the *actual* cost of the backfill strategy (internal promotion first, external hiring for the residual), and the training bill reflects the drifting occupancy. All figures in sigma per the problem's convention that decisions are made on the relative value of sigma.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recruit: RC = sum_k c_k * (number of external hires at level k over 24 months), c = (1.2, 0.7, 0.6, 0.6, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3) sigma for (senior, junior, supexp, supinex, empexp, empinex, clerk) — table1.csv. Training: TC = sum_k tr_k * sum_{t=1..24} O_k(t)/12, tr = (0.5, 0.6, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 0.05) sigma/yr. Salary (context, not a talent-management line but reported for scale): SC = sum_k s_k * sum_t O_k(t)/12, s = (8, 4, 2, 1.5, 1, 0.9, 0.9) sigma/yr. Executed in code/model.py at 18%/yr, 24 months.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2-year talent-management budget at the observed 18% churn: recruiting = 15.0 sigma (external hires only — internal promotion is free of recruiting cost but carries the ramp penalty), training = 127.4 sigma, total talent management = 142.4 sigma over 2 years (~71 sigma/yr). For scale, total payroll over the same 24 months is 789.7 sigma, so talent management is ~18% of the people budget, with training dominating recruiting 8.5:1 — the budget story is that ICM is a training-cost business in disguise, because every churn cycle re-trains a fresh cohort at 70% productivity. Sensitivity: at 25%/yr recruiting rises to 15.9 sigma over 2 years (more external backfill of deeper mid-level holes at higher per-hire cost) while training falls to 113.2 sigma (fewer occupied seats) — the mix shifts toward recruiting as churn accelerates. At 35%/yr: recruiting 19.3 sigma, training 103.6 sigma. The hiring capacity constraint means the recruiting line is capped: ICM physically cannot hire its way out of a churn spike, which is why the budget question and the sustainability question (Task 4) are the same question.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain its 80%-full position status if the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%? To 35%? What are the costs and indirect effects of these higher turnover rates?
tasks.task_analysis: Sustainability test: run the 24-month simulation at uniform 25%/yr and 35%/yr churn (all levels), with the same capacity-limited hiring, and check whether the fill rate holds at or above 0.80. The answer is determined by the balance between annual exit flow (churn rate x occupied) and the hiring channel's ceiling (9% of positions per year, 2/3 of vacancies): sustainability requires churn <= hiring capacity plus internal-promotion recovery, which is nowhere near 25%.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Scenarios: S25 with all-level annual rate 0.25; S35 with 0.35; reference S18 at 0.18 (code/model.py, --sweep base=0.18,0.25,0.35). Metrics: mean fill rate in each year, minimum fill, mean productivity as % of the fully-staffed-at-85% baseline P0, 2-year recruiting and training cost, total quits.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: No, ICM cannot hold 80% full at either rate. At 25%/yr: mean fill falls to 75.4% in year 1 and 61.1% in year 2, minimum 54.6% — a 45-position hole in the second year. At 35%/yr: 70.3% in year 1, 49.6% in year 2, minimum 41.6% — ICM would be under half-staffed within two years. (For reference, even at the current 18% the model drifts to ~72% by year 2, so 80% is already a target, not a guaranteed state.) Costs: recruiting rises from 15.0 (18%) to 15.9 (25%) to 19.3 (35%) sigma over 2 years — the per-hire mix shifts up-level as middle seats open; training falls from 127.4 to 113.2 to 103.6 sigma because fewer seats are occupied; total quits 121 -> 171 -> 223 over 2 years. Productivity: 94.7%/83.8% of baseline (year 1/year 2) at 18%, 88.3%/74.6% at 25%, 83.3%/65.2% at 35% — i.e., at 35% churn the organization is producing at about two-thirds of its capacity-staffed output in year 2. Indirect effects: (i) self-reinforcement — the morale-overwork feedback adds vacancy-proportional quit risk, so the decline accelerates past the point where fill drops ~15 points below capacity; (ii) quality erosion on the ~6-month lag becomes visible within the 2-year window at 35% (defects surface as overworked staff stop compensating); (iii) the promotion pool is hollowed out — at 35% the qualified pool for junior/senior seats turns over faster than the 3-5 year tenure requirement can replenish it, so ICM either staffs management with unready internal candidates or exceeds its (already small) external hiring capacity; (iv) the churn rate itself is unstable: with 85% quit-dominated departures and contagion, a 35% rate fed by dissatisfaction will not stay at 35% — the model's cap of 2x contagion understates a full-runaway scenario, so 35% should be read as 'the rate the CEO fears', under which the organization halves its effective staffing in two years, not as a stable operating point.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate the impact of 30% churn in both junior managers and experienced supervisors (all other levels at 18%) for the next two years, under (1) no external recruiting and (2) promoting only qualified employees; explain the impact on HR health.
tasks.task_analysis: This is the 'middle-management hemorrhage' scenario: the two middle tiers (45 positions: 20 junior managers + 25 experienced supervisors) churn at 30%/yr — already above the problem's stated 2x-average = 36%? No: 30% is the supervisor's chosen stress value, below the current 36% observed for mid-levels but far above the company 18% — while the rest of the company churns at 18%. Two constraints are imposed simultaneously: no external recruiting at all (all backfill must come from internal promotion), and only tenure-qualified incumbents are eligible for promotion. The scenario directly tests whether the internal ladder can absorb a mid-level exodus, which it cannot, because the ladder's inflow to these tiers is the 15%/yr and 8%/yr promotion of lower levels — less than half the 30%/yr outflow — and the qualified-only rule further throttles the inflow by restricting it to the subset of incumbents who have satisfied the multi-year tenure requirement.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Scenario T30: annual rates junior = supexp = 0.30, all other levels = 0.18; external hiring disabled; promotion pool restricted to qualified incumbents (code/model.py, qualified-promotion flag, no-external flag, 24 months). Comparison scenario T30free: same churn, external hiring allowed, no qualification restriction, to isolate what the two constraints cost. Metrics: fill rate by year and minimum, productivity as % of baseline, 2-year recruiting/training cost, total quits.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: With no external recruiting and qualified-only promotion, the organization loses 127 people over 2 years (30% churn in the middle tiers plus 18% elsewhere) and the fill rate collapses: 73.2% mean in year 1, 56.0% in year 2, minimum 50.8% — below the Task 4 35%-everywhere case (54.6% minimum) despite lower total churn, because the damage is concentrated exactly where the ladder's recovery is slowest. Productivity: 88.3% of baseline in year 1, 70.2% in year 2. Recruiting cost is 0 sigma (no external hiring) but this is a false economy: the 0.7-1.2 sigma per-hire savings are dwarfed by the productivity hole, and training falls to 106.8 sigma with payroll to 699.4 sigma (unfilled seats). The contrast scenario (30% mid-level churn *with* external hiring and no qualification rule) holds 79.5%/69.6% fill with minimum 67.0% — so the two constraints cost roughly 13 fill points in year 2. HR-health diagnosis: (1) the middle-management pipeline is structurally incapable of self-repair — the ladder delivers ~3-4 promotions/year into junior managers while 30% of 20 seats is ~6 exits/year before promotion even offsets anything, so the deficit compounds every month; (2) qualified-only promotion, while correct policy in calm times, is a poison pill in a hemorrhage: it keeps the unready out but leaves the seats empty, and the problem's own tenure requirement (issue 6) is what makes the pool thin; (3) the empty middle tiers cascade — with 50 supervisors managing 500 subordinates, each supervisor vacancy spreads overwork to ~10 subordinates, which feeds the morale-overwork term and raises quit risk in the *employee* tiers (the contagion channel of Task 2), so a middle-tier exodus is a company-wide productivity event, not a local HR problem; (4) the practical reading for the supervisor: 30% mid-level churn with no external recruiting is not survivable over two years — the organization halves its effective management capacity — and the levers are (a) restoring even a partial external hiring channel for the two middle tiers (the 13 fill points the contrast scenario recovers), (b) temporarily relaxing the tenure requirement for promotion (the qualified pool is the binding constraint), and (c) retention investment in the two tiers, since Task 3 showed training/retention spend is where the budget actually is.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multi-layered networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human Capital network to other organizational network layers (information flow, trust, influence, friendship).
tasks.task_analysis: The HR manager's vision is a multilayer organizational network in the sense of the Kivelä et al. (2013) framework the problem cites: the same set of 370 nodes carrying multiple relation layers, with intra-layer edges and inter-layer (same-node) projections. Team science (Salas et al. 2008; Stokols et al. 2008) supplies the content — teamwork is a mediator between structure and performance, so the network must encode not just who is employed but how work is actually shared. The model from Tasks 1-2 already instantiates three layers (reporting R, work W, informal I); the extension is to add the layers the other offices are building and define how they couple.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Layer plan: R (reporting, directed tree, Task 1), W (work/Erdos-Renyi, Task 1), I (informal/friendship, preferential attachment, Task 1), plus proposed layers T (trust), F (information flow, directed), U (influence, directed, weighted). Coupling rules: (1) intra-layer dynamics — churn contagion (Task 2) runs on the union W ∪ I, with tie-strength from I modulating the 0.3 transfer and the 6-month decay; influence U is derived as the weighted in-neighborhood on R (a manager's influence is its span) plus W (peer influence), so U is partly endogenous to the layers already modeled; (2) inter-layer projection — the same-node coupling matrix C of Kivelä et al. is here near-identity (same positions, same people), so the interesting structure is in the edge-discrepancy: nodes where R-degree, W-degree and I-degree disagree are structurally isolated (high R-degree, low W/I-degree) and are exactly the churn-risk candidates the HR manager wants flagged early (issue 1); (3) team-science overlay — cluster the work layer into teams (community detection on W); per team, track cohesion (internal W-edge density), leadership load (R-degree concentration), and churn incidence; Salas et al.'s finding that coordination overhead and shared mental models mediate performance maps directly onto 'team output = sum of member output x team-cohesion factor', which is the team-level refinement of the level-aggregated productivity equation in Task 2; (4) the HR office leads because R, W and I are all HR-owned data (rosters, schedules, evaluations), while T/F/U require the other offices' sensors — the network is the integration contract: each office contributes one layer, HR owns the node set and the churn model that consumes all layers. Concretely, the annual-evaluation ratings (issue 3, currently unused) become the natural weights on R-edges and seeds for U, and the churn-risk score from Task 2 becomes a standing HR dashboard output: risk(v) = base-level-rate x (1 + contagion from W∪I neighbors) x (1 - evaluation-adjusted trust), updated monthly.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What this buys: (1) early churn detection (issue 1) — risk is a per-node function of layer degrees and neighbor churn, computable before any exit, so loyalty investment can be targeted at high-risk, low-tenure nodes exactly as the HR manager intends; (2) the 'churn diffuses' observation (issue 2) becomes a measurable quantity — contagion strength and decay (0.3, 6 months, Task 2) can be estimated from the network's own history once exits are logged against W∪I, closing the calibration loop; (3) position-matching (issue 3) — evaluations weighted on R-edges let HR see which seats are staffed below their evaluation, feeding the qualified-pool logic of Task 5 with real data; (4) the middle-management trap (issues 4 and 6) is visible as a layer phenomenon: the middle tiers have high R-degree (they are where the tree branches) but, in the Task 1 realization, also high W-degree without corresponding I-degree growth — structurally busy, socially thin, which is a network signature of the 'stuck' feeling that drives their 2x churn. Limitations: inter-layer weights (how much trust modulates contagion, how much influence adds to quit risk) are not yet calibrated — the exchanges calibrated the single-layer contagion, not the cross-layer couplings, so those should be read as structural hypotheses to be fitted once the other offices' layers exist; community detection results are sensitive to the work layer's homogeneity assumption from Task 1; and the whole construction inherits the Task 1 limitation that node identity is by position, so a departure-and-refill breaks the layer histories at that node (the multilayer history should be keyed to the person, which the HR office's existing records can support). The practical near-term step is small: keep logging exits with their W∪I neighborhoods against the Task 1 network — that single log is enough to estimate the contagion parameters and to validate the whole multilayer vision before any other office's layer is built.
